name: Yujin Kim, Ph.D.
title: Postdoctoral Research Fellow
address: 2800 Plymouth Rd, NCRC B20-301W, Ann Arbor, MI 48109
tagline: I am an immune engineer designing nanobiomaterials for vaccines and immunotherapies.
bio:
I am a postdoctoral research fellow in the Department of Pharmaceutical Sciences at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor.

I received my Ph.D. in 2021 from the Department of Biological Sciences at KAIST, under the supervision of Prof. Sangyong Jon. During my doctoral training, I added materials design and engineering to a background in the life sciences, developing nanomaterial-based vaccines and immunotherapeutics.

Since joining Prof. James J. Moon's group at the University of Michigan in 2023, I have deepened the immunological reasoning behind the materials I design and developed the independence to lead my own line of research in in vivo immune cell engineering.

Together, these two stages define how I work as an immune engineer at the interface of immunology, nanotechnology, and biomedical engineering.

research_interests.title: Engineering Nanomaterial Delivery Platforms
research_interests.description: Designing lipid- and protein-based nanoparticles through rational and data-driven design

research_interests.title: Targeted Delivery of Immune Modulators
research_interests.description: Directing nucleic acids, antigens, and immunomodulatory agents to the organs and cells where they act

research_interests.title: In Vivo Immune Cell Engineering
research_interests.description: Engineering dendritic cells, T cells, and macrophages directly in the body to reprogram their function

research_interests.title: Development of Vaccines and Immunotherapies
research_interests.description: Translating these platforms into preventive and therapeutic strategies for cancer, infection, and autoimmunity

research_interests_tagline: Engineering nanomaterials to control where and how the immune system is instructed in vivo.

research_themes.title: Nanomaterial Platforms for Immune Delivery
research_themes.description: Biocompatible nanomaterials — lipid nanoparticles, liposomes, and self-assembled protein nanostructures — engineered so that their physicochemical design governs where a payload travels and how the immune system reads it. Published work includes self-assembling protein nanobarrels that present antigen without a separate adjuvant.

research_themes.title: Delivery of mRNA and Biopharmaceuticals
research_themes.description: Lipid nanoparticle design for mRNA and other biologics, focused on the steps that limit potency in the body: cellular uptake, endosomal escape, and tissue distribution. Ongoing work extends this to computational and AI-guided approaches to nanoparticle design.

research_themes.title: In Vivo Immune Cell Engineering
research_themes.description: Reprogramming dendritic cells, T cells, and macrophages directly inside the body rather than ex vivo, using targeted delivery to reach a chosen immune-cell population — including in situ approaches to chimeric antigen receptor macrophages for solid tumors.

research_themes.title: Vaccines and Immunotherapy for Intractable Disease
research_themes.description: Translating these platforms into therapies: cancer nanovaccines sequenced with checkpoint blockade, neoantigen- and tumor-stroma-targeted vaccines, modular vaccine platforms against infectious disease, and nanomedicines that calm autoimmune inflammation.
